parole.testo: From Middle High German -ec, -ic, from Old High German -ig, from Proto-West Germanic *-g, from Proto-Germanic *-gaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos.

Cognate with English -some and Dutch -zaam. Related also to Old High German samo (“the same”) and sama (“similary”).

Middle High German -schaft, from Old High German -skaft, -skaf, from Proto-West Germanic *-skapi. Cognate with Dutch -schap, Swedish -skap, English -ship, Danish -skab, West Frisian -skip. Final -t possibly from Proto-Germanic *-þiz, as seen in *gaskaftiz.

parole.significato: A suffix used to derive abstract nouns: -dom
parole.testo: From Middle High German -tuom, from Old High German -tuom, from Proto-West Germanic *-dōm, from Proto-Germanic *-dōmaz (“-dom”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos (“thing put”). Cognate with English -dom, Dutch -dom, Danish -dom, Swedish -dom.

From wert, from Middle High German wert, from Old High German werd, from Proto-West Germanic *werþ, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz.
From Middle High German ar, arn, from Old High German aro, arn, from Proto-West Germanic *arō, from Proto-Germanic *arô.

parole.significato: Separable verb prefix that indicates removal or quitting, off, away.
parole.testo: From ab, from Middle High German abe, ab, from Old High German ab, from Proto-West Germanic *ab(a), from Proto-Germanic *ab. Compare English off-.

parole.significato: evening; the time from dusk until midnight
parole.testo: From Middle High German ābent, from Old High German āband, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþ, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs. Compare Low German Avend, Dutch avond, English even (evening), Old Norse aptann, Swedish afton, Norwegian and Danish aften. Compare English eve.

parole.significato: evening star; the planet Venus as seen in the western sky in the evening
parole.testo: From Middle High German ābentsterne, from Old High German ābandsterno, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþsternō, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþsternǭ. Equivalent to Abend (“evening”) + Stern (“star”).

parole.significato: to give up, relinquish, let go, concede, hand over, etc. (power, money, valuable objects, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old High German *abegëben, from Old High German abagëban, from Proto-West Germanic *abageban, from Proto-Germanic *abagebaną; equivalent to ab- (“from”) + geben (“give”).

From Middle High German abescheiden, from Old High German abaskeidan, from Proto-West Germanic *abaskaiþan, from Proto-Germanic *abaskaiþaną. Equivalent to ab- + scheiden. Cognates include Dutch afscheiden, Old English ofscēadan and Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌽 (afskaidan).

From Middle High German abeziehen, abziehen, from Old High German abaziohan, from Proto-West Germanic *abateuhan, from Proto-Germanic *abateuhaną; compare Middle Dutch aftien, Old Saxon aftiohan, Old English oftēon, Gothic 𐌰𐍆𐍄𐌹𐌿𐌷𐌰𐌽 (aftiuhan). By surface analysis, ab- + ziehen.

parole.significato: eight (numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 8; or describing a set with eight elements)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ahte, from Old High German ahto, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtō, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Dutch acht, English eight, Danish otte, Swedish åtta, Greek οκτώ (októ), Latin octō.
From Middle High German ahtode, from Old High German ahtodo, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtudō. Equivalent to acht + -te.
From Middle High German āle, Old High German āla, from Proto-West Germanic *ālu, from Proto-Germanic *ēlō.

From Middle High German anen, from Old High German *anōn, from Proto-West Germanic *anōn, from *ana (“on”, preposition), from Proto-Germanic *an (“on”). From Middle High German alb, alp, from Old High German alp, from Proto-West Germanic *albi, from Proto-Germanic *albiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós. Doublet of Elf, borrowed from English later.

Substantivized neuter singular of the adjective all (“all”), without pronominal ending; from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz. Present meaning “cosmos” from the 2nd half of the 17th century onwards.
From Middle High German al, from Old High German al, from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz.

parole.testo: From Middle High German anehaben, anhaben, from Old High German anahabēn, from Proto-West Germanic *anahabbjan, from Proto-Germanic *anahabjaną. Equivalent to an- + haben. Compare Dutch aanhebben, English have on, Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (anahaban).
From Middle High German anker, from Old High German anker, ankero, from Proto-West Germanic *ankurō, from Proto-Germanic *ankurô.

From Middle High German anekomen, from Old High German anaqueman, from Proto-West Germanic *anakweman, from Proto-Germanic *anakwemaną (“to come to, come at, arrive”). Compare Dutch aankomen, English oncome, Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌵𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽 (anaqiman).

From Middle High German anleiten, aneleiten, from Old High German analeiten, from Proto-West Germanic *analaidijan, from Proto-Germanic *analaidijaną. Equivalent to an- + leiten. Cognates include Dutch aanleiden and English onlead.
From Middle High German antlitze, from Old High German antlizzi, from Proto-West Germanic *andawliti, from Proto-Germanic *andawlitją. Compare Swedish anlete.

parole.significato: toil, regularly performed work, regularly pursued economic activity, labor, job, employment, occupation
parole.testo: From Middle High German arbeit, from Old High German arbeit, from Proto-West Germanic *arbaiþi, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan, servant, slave”), from which English orphan is also derived. Cognate with Yiddish אַרבעט (arbet), Middle English arve

From Middle High German art, from Old High German *art, from Proto-West Germanic *ard, from Proto-Germanic *ardiz.

From Middle High German ast, from Old High German ast, from Proto-West Germanic *ast, from Proto-Germanic *astaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ósdos (“branch”).

From Middle High German ouge, from Old High German ouga, from Proto-West Germanic *augā, from Proto-Germanic *augô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Modern cognates include Alemannic German Aug, Bavarian Aug, Dutch oog, English eye, Icelandic auga, Swedish öga.

From Middle High German ackes, from Old High German ackus, itself from Proto-West Germanic *akusi, while ultimately descending from Proto-Germanic *akwisī. Compare Low German Ax, Dutch aks, English axe, Danish økse, Swedish yxa, Icelandic öxi.

From Middle High German bach m or f, from Old High German bah, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Cognate with Dutch beek, English beach and beck. From Middle High German bat, from Old High German bad, from Proto-West Germanic *baþ, from Proto-Germanic *baþą. Related to bähen.

parole.significato: ball (round or roundish object, most commonly used in games)

From Middle High German bant, from Old High German bant, from Proto-West Germanic *band n or m, from Proto-Germanic *bandą ~ *bandaz (“band, bond”), derived from *bindaną (“to bind”). The noun was neuter in most of High German, but masculine in Low German (see Middle Low German bant m) and parts of
From Middle High German and Old High German banc, bank (“height”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz. Related to Old Saxon bank.

parole.testo: From Middle High German bannen, from Old High German bannan, from Proto-West Germanic *bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.

From Middle High German base, from Old High German basa, from Proto-West Germanic *baswā, from Proto-Germanic *baswǭ (“father's sister; paternal aunt”). Compare Saterland Frisian Bääsje (“grandmother”), Dutch baas (“master; boss”). More at boss.
From Middle High German būwen, from Old High German būan, from Proto-West Germanic *būan, from Proto-Germanic *būaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, the athematic root aorist of the root *bʰuH-.

From Middle High German būre, gebūre, from Old High German būr (“peasant”), gibūr, gibūro. All these forms ultimately descend from Proto-West Germanic *būr, itself from Proto-Germanic *būraz (“inhabitant, dweller”). Compare English boor.
From Middle High German boum, from Old High German boum, from Proto-West Germanic *baum, from Proto-Germanic *baumaz. Akin to Dutch boom, Low German Boom, West Frisian beam, English beam.
From Middle High German biben, from Old High German bibēn, from Proto-West Germanic *bibēn, from Proto-Germanic *bibāną. The modern vocalism is from Middle Low German beven, from Old Saxon bibōn.

From Middle High German bedenken, from Old High German pidenken, bidenken, bithenken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþankijan, from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną, equivalent to be- + denken. Cognate with English bethink, Dutch bedenken.

From Middle High German bette, bete, bet, from Old High German betti, beti (“bed, flower-bed”), from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją. Doublet of Bett (“bed for sleeping”). parole.significato: meet, to encounter, to come across

parole.significato: to begin; to commence; to be started
parole.testo: From Middle High German beginnen, from Old High German biginnan, from Proto-West Germanic *biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną. Cognate with Low German beginnen, Dutch beginnen, West Frisian begjinne, and English begin.
From Middle High German bī, from Old High German bī, from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi. More at by.

parole.significato: leg of a person, animal, or object
parole.testo: From Middle High German bein, from Old High German bein, from Proto-West Germanic *bain, from Proto-Germanic *bainą. Compare Dutch been, English bone, Danish ben.

From Middle High German bīȥen, from Old High German bīȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bītan, from Proto-Germanic *bītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydt (“to split”). Cognate with Dutch bijten, Low German bieten, English bite, Danish bide, Swedish bita.

From Middle High German bekomen, from Old High German biqueman, bikweman, from Proto-West Germanic *bikweman, from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną, equivalent to be- + kommen. Cognate to Dutch bekomen, English become.

From Middle High German belche, from Old High German belihha f, belihho m, from Proto-West Germanic *balikō, from Proto-Germanic *balikô (“coot”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“white; to shine, gleam”). Cognate with Old Saxon beliko (“coot”), Latin fulica (“coot”).

parole.testo: From Middle High German benëmen, from Old High German binëman, from Proto-West Germanic *bineman, from Proto-Germanic *binemaną. Equivalent to be- + nehmen. Compare English benim.

From Middle High German benetzen, from Old High German binezzen, derived from nezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *nattjan, from Proto-Germanic *natjaną, from *nataz (“wet”), whence German nass. parole.significato: a club wielded as a weapon
parole.testo: From Middle High German bengel, from Old High German *bengil (“club", "stick", "hammer”), from Proto-West Germanic *bangil, from Proto-Germanic *bangilaz (“club, hammer”), from Proto-Germanic *bang- (“to beat”).
From Middle High German bereite, from Old High German bireiti, reiti; from Proto-West Germanic *raidī, from the Proto-Germanic base *raidaz (“ready”). Cognate with English ready, Vilamovian byrat.

From Middle High German bërc, from Old High German bërg, itself from Proto-West Germanic *berg, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. Compare Dutch berg, German Low German Barg, Berg, Biärg, West Frisian berch, English berry, barrow, Danish bjerg, Swedish berg.

parole.testo: From Middle High German bet, bette, from Old High German betti, from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją (“plot, grave, resting-place, bed”). Cognate with Low German Bedd, Dutch bed, West Frisian bêd, English bed, Swedish bädd, Icelandic beður. Doublet of Beet.

From Early New High German beugel, from an unattested diminutive of Middle High German bouc, boug- (“ring, bracelet”), from Old High German boug (“ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *baug, from Proto-Germanic *baugaz (“ring”). From Middle High German bewenden, from Old High German biwenten, from Proto-West Germanic *biwandijan, from Proto-Germanic *biwandijaną (“to turn around”), equivalent to be- + wenden. Cognate with English bewend.

parole.significato: to bend something (to form something into a curve)
parole.testo: From Middle High German biegen, from Old High German biogan, from Proto-West Germanic *beugan, from Proto-Germanic *beuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to bend”).

parole.significato: beer (alcoholic beverage fermented from starch material; a serving of this beverage)
parole.testo: From Middle High German bier, from Old High German bior, from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰews-, *bheus- (“dross, sediment, brewer's yeast”). Akin to Dutch bier, Low German Beer, bêr, English beer, Icelandic bjór. More at beer.

From Middle High German bieten, from Old High German biotan, from Proto-West Germanic *beudan, from Proto-Germanic *beudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“be awake, aware”). Compare Low German bieden, beden, Dutch bieden, English bid, bede, Danish byde, Swedish bjuda.

parole.significato: to bind, to tie, to fasten something by means of a string etc.
parole.testo: From Middle High German binden, from Old High German bintan, from Proto-West Germanic *bindan, from Proto-Germanic *bindaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-. Cognate with Low German binnen, binden, Dutch binden, English bind, Danish binde.

From Middle High German birke, from Old High German birka, bircha, from Proto-West Germanic *birkijā. The Old High German variant birihha shows a svarabhakti vowel; if continued it would have led to modern *Birche (compare Kirche). Cognate to Dutch berk, Low German Bark, English birch, Swedish björk

parole.significato: bite (instance or way of biting; wound from biting)
parole.testo: From Middle High German biȥ, from Old High German biȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *biti, from Proto-Germanic *bitiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”). parole.significato: to ask, to beg, to plead, to bid, to request
parole.testo: From Middle High German bitten, from Old High German bitten, from Proto-West Germanic *biddjan, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną. Compare Low German bidden, Dutch bidden, English bid, Danish bede.
From Middle High German blāsen, from Old High German blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan.

parole.significato: leaf (green and flat organ of a plant)
parole.testo: From Middle High German blat, plat, from Old High German blat, from Proto-West Germanic *blad (“leaf”), from Proto-Germanic *bladą (“leaf”); akin to Low German Blatt, Dutch blad, English blade, Danish and Swedish blad. Indo-European cognates include Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon), Latin folium.
From Middle High German blā (genitive blāwes), from Old High German blāo, from Proto-West Germanic *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz.
From Middle High German blëch, from Old High German blëh, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką. Compare Old Saxon blek, Dutch blik.

From a merger of Middle High German bleichen, from Old High German bleihhen, from Proto-West Germanic *blaikijan, from Proto-Germanic *blaikijaną, and Middle High German blīchen, from Old High German blīhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *blīkan, from Proto-Germanic *blīkaną. Related to bleich. Cognate

parole.significato: blaze (white or lighter-coloured marking on a horse's face)
parole.testo: Middle High German blasse, Old High German blassa, from Proto-West Germanic *blasī, from Proto-Germanic *blasį̄. Cognate with Dutch bles.

parole.significato: to look (usually in a certain direction toward something)
parole.testo: From Middle High German blicken, from Old High German blicchen, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką (“look”).

From Middle High German blōȥ, from Old High German blōȥ (“bare, naked”), from Proto-West Germanic *blaut, from Proto-Germanic *blautaz (“void, emaciated, soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlaw- (“weak, frightened”). Cognate with Dutch bloot (“bare, naked”), Danish blød (“soft, weak”), Danish blot (

parole.significato: flower, blossom (colorful, conspicuous reproductive structure(s) of an angiosperm)
parole.testo: From Middle High German bluome, from Old High German bluomo, from Proto-West Germanic *blōmō (“flower”).

From Middle High German bluot, from Old High German bluot, from Proto-West Germanic *blōd, from Proto-Germanic *blōþą, of uncertain origin. Cognates include Bavarian Bluat, Low German Bloot, Dutch bloed, English blood, Danish and Swedish blod and Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐍉𐌸 (blōþ).
From Middle High German bluoten, from Old High German bluoten, bluotēn, from Proto-West Germanic *blōdijan.

parole.significato: synonym of aufblähen (“to inflate, puff up, balloon”)
parole.testo: From Middle High German blæjen, from Old High German blāen, from Proto-West Germanic *blāan, from Proto-Germanic *blēaną. Cognate with obsolete Dutch blaaien, English blow.

parole.significato: buck, ram; the male of certain animals, especially goat, sheep, and roedeer
parole.testo: From Middle High German bok, from Old High German bok, from Proto-West Germanic *bukk. Cognate with Bavarian Bock, Danish buk, Dutch bok, English buck, Norwegian bukk, and Swedish bock.

From Middle High German boden, bodem, from Old High German bodam, from Proto-West Germanic *bodm, from Proto-Germanic *budm-, a variant of *butmaz (whence English bottom, which see for more), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn. Cognate with English bottom, Dutch bodem, Hunsrik Boddem. Doublet of Bod
From Middle High German boge, from Old High German bogo, from Proto-West Germanic *bogō, from Proto-Germanic *bugô. Compare Dutch boog, English bow, Danish bue, Norwegian Nynorsk boge, Swedish båge.

From Middle High German bone, from Old High German bōna, from Proto-West Germanic *baunu, from Proto-Germanic *baunō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ- (“bean”). Compare Danish bønne, Dutch boon, English bean, Low German Bohn, West Frisian bean.
From Middle High German bōȥen, from Old High German bōȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *bautan, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to strike”). Cognate with English beat, which see.

From Middle High German botschaft, boteschaft, from Old High German botoscaft, from Proto-West Germanic *bodaskapi, from Proto-Germanic *budaskapiz. By surface analysis, Bote + -schaft. Cognate with German Low German Böskupp, Dutch boodschap (whence also Afrikaans boodskap and Sranan Tongo boskopu),

From Middle High German brā (inflected brāw-; rarely also brāwe), from Old High German brāwa (late also brā), from Proto-West Germanic *brāwu, from Proto-Germanic *brēwō. Cognate with Dutch brauw, English brow.

parole.significato: bride; a woman taking part in a marriage
parole.testo: From Middle High German brūt, from Old High German brūt (akin to Old Saxon brūd), from Proto-West Germanic *brūdi, from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz. Compare Dutch bruid, English bride, Danish brud.

From Middle High German brëchen, from Old High German brëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-. Akin to Old Saxon brekan, Dutch breken (“to break”), English break.
From Middle High German breit, from Old High German breit, from Proto-West Germanic *braid, from Proto-Germanic *braidaz.

From Middle High German brët, from Old High German brët, from Proto-West Germanic *bred, from Proto-Germanic *bredą, an e-grade byform of *burdą (“board, plank”). Cognate with Old English bred and Yiddish ברעט (bret).

parole.significato: to bring, to fetch, to take, to convey, to bear
parole.testo: From Middle High German bringen, from Old High German bringan, from Proto-West Germanic *bringan, from Proto-Germanic *bringaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenk-. Compare Hunsrik bringe, Low German brengen, Dutch brengen, Afrikaans bring, English bring, West Frisian bringe, Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌲𐌰𐌽 (briggan)

From Middle High German brōt, from Old High German brōt (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *braud, from Proto-Germanic *braudą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrew- (“to seethe, to boil”). Originally, the meaning of Brot was "what has been fermented, leaven" and may be a nominal
From Middle High German bruoder, from Old High German bruoder, from Proto-West Germanic *brōþer, from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr. Doublet of Frater.

From Middle High German brunne, from Old High German brunno, from Proto-West Germanic *brunnō, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô, whence also Old English burna, Old Norse brunnr; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrun- (“a bubbling forth; a fountain, wellspring, source”). The form is Upper German, mos

parole.significato: book (collection of sheets of paper bound together to hinge at one edge; long work fit for publication)
parole.testo: From Middle High German buoch, from Old High German buoh, from Proto-West Germanic *bōk, from Proto-Germanic *bōks. Cognate with English book.

From Middle High German buochstabe, from Old High German *buohstabo (“letter, writing”) (attested only as Old High German buohstab; > German Buchstab), from Proto-West Germanic *bōkstabō, from Proto-Germanic *bōkstabô, a variant of *bōkstabaz. Compare English bookstaff, bookstave.

From Middle High German buode, from Old High German *buoda, from Proto-West Germanic *bōþu, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō. Probably related to *būaną (“to build”), whence German bauen. Cognate with Middle Dutch boede, Middle Low German bôde, Old Norse búð, bóð, whence English booth.

parole.significato: bow, prow (of a ship), nose (of an aircraft)
parole.testo: From Middle High German buoc (“animal shoulder”), from Old High German buog (“animal shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōgu, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz (“arm; shoulder”). More at English bough. The common contemporary meaning “bow” (early 17th c.) is a semantic loan from Middle Low German bôch,

From Middle High German burc, from Old High German burg, from Proto-West Germanic *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérǵʰ-s, a form of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fortified elevation”). Compare Dutch burcht, English borough, ‑bury, Danish borg.
From Middle High German busch, bosch, from Old High German busk, from Proto-West Germanic *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. Compare Dutch bos, English bush, Danish busk.

From Middle High German bër m, Old High German bëro m, from Proto-West Germanic *berō, from Proto-Germanic *berô, conventionally taken to be a taboo-avoidance term derived from the word for "brown". Compare Dutch beer, English bear, West Frisian bear, Danish bjørn.

From Middle High German bœse, bōse, from Old High German bōsi, from Proto-West Germanic *bausī, from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“inflated, puffed up, arrogant, bad”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bew- (“to blow, inflate, swell”), akin to Yiddish בייז (beyz), Dutch boos, and English boast.

From Middle High German bürste, plural (and dative/genitive singular) of burst, from Old High German *burst (“bristle”, attested as plural burste, pursti), from Proto-West Germanic *bursti, from Proto-Germanic *burstiz. Compare related Borste (“bristle”).

From Middle High German bütel, butel, from Old High German butil (“court official, messenger”), from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz (“herald, messenger”), from Proto-Germanic *beudaną (“to announce, present, offer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to make aware”). Inherited from Middle High German dach, from Old High German dah, from Proto-West Germanic *þak, from Proto-Germanic *þaką, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg-. From Middle High German danken, from Old High German dankōn. Compare Dutch danken, English thank, Danish takke.

parole.significato: to lack, to have a need (particularly in terms of food: to starve)
parole.testo: From Proto-West Germanic *þarbēn, from Proto-Germanic *þarbāną.

From Middle High German darm, from Old High German darm, from Proto-West Germanic *þarm, from Proto-Germanic *þarmaz. Cognate with Old Norse þarmr (whence Danish tarm), obsolete English tharms (“twisted guts”). Compare Ancient Greek τόρμος (tórmos, “hole”).
From Middle High German dehsele, from Old High German dehsala, thehsala, from Proto-West Germanic *þehsulā, from Proto-Germanic *þehsulǭ (“axe”). Cognate with Dutch dissel, Old Norse þexla.

parole.significato: any cloth or cushion used as a covering; a tablecloth, blanket, quilt, duvet, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle High German decke, from Old High German theckī, decchī, derived from thecken (modern decken), from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Cognate with English deck. Compare analogous Dutch dek. Also related with German Dach, Dutch dak, English thatch.

parole.significato: to stretch, to make longer or wider by pulling, pushing, extending
parole.testo: From Middle High German denen, dennen, from Old High German thenen, thennen, from Proto-West Germanic *þannjan, from Proto-Germanic *þanjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch”). The simple -n- was generalised from certain inflected forms of the West Germanic verb. Cognate with Gothic 𐌿𐍆𐌸𐌰
From Middle High German dīhsel, from Old High German dīhsala, from Proto-West Germanic *þīhslu, from Proto-Germanic *þinhslō.

From Middle High German denken, from Old High German denken, thenken, from Proto-West Germanic *þankijan, from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng-. Cognate with Bavarian denkn, denka, Dutch denken, dinken, Low German denken, dinken, West Frisian tinke, English think, Icelandic

parole.significato: to interpret (e.g. dreams), to understand, to read (e.g. signs)
parole.testo: From Middle High German diuten, from Old High German diuten, from Proto-West Germanic *þiudijan, from Proto-Germanic *þiudijaną, derived from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”), whence also comes Old English þēod (“people, nation”). Cognate with Dutch duiden, Icelandic þýða (“translate”), Swedish tyda

parole.significato: German (of or pertaining to the German people)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German diutisch, diutsch, tiutsch, from Old High German diutisk (“popular, vernacular”), from Proto-West Germanic *þiudisk, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of the people, popular”), an adjective from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”, whence Old English þeod, Icelandic þjóð

From Middle High German dīchte, from Old High German dīhti, from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. From Middle High German diep, Old High German diob, from Proto-West Germanic *þeub, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz. Cognate with Old Norse þýfð, Old English þēof, Dutch dief, English thief, Gothic 𐌸𐌹𐌿𐍆𐍃 (þiufs).

From Middle High German dingen, from Old High German dingōn, from Proto-West Germanic *þingōn (“to hold a meeting”), from Proto-Germanic *þingōną. Originally a weak verb, which developed secondary strong forms; a process that seems to have begun in the Middle Low German cognate. Compare Dutch dingen

From Middle High German distel, from Old High German distil, from Proto-West Germanic *þistil, from Proto-Germanic *þistilaz, which see for cognates. parole.significato: yes; surely; really; on the contrary
parole.testo: From Middle High German doch, from Old High German doh, from Proto-West Germanic *þauh, from Proto-Germanic *þauh. Cognate to Old English þēah (English though).

parole.significato: village (rural habitation of size between a hamlet and a town)
parole.testo: From Middle High German dorf, from Old High German dorf, thorph, from Proto-West Germanic *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą. Doublet of Truppe (English troop). Cognate with Old Dutch thorp (modern Dutch dorp), Old Saxon thorp, Old English þorp (archaic English thorp).

From Middle High German drāt (“wire, thread”), from Old High German drāt, thrāt, from Proto-West Germanic *þrādu, from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *treh₁-tu-, from *terh₁- (“rub, twist”). Related to drehen (“to turn, twist”), with which it was still associated in early modern Ge

From Middle High German dræjen, dræhen, from Old High German drāen (akin to Old Saxon thrāian), from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną. Cognate with Bavarian drahn, Dutch draaien and English throw.

parole.significato: three (numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 3; or describing a set with three elements)
parole.testo: From Middle High German drī, from Old High German dri, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Dutch drie, English three, Danish tre.
From Middle High German droschel, from Old High German throskela, from Proto-West Germanic *þrosklā, *þrostlā (“thrush”).

parole.significato: to push, press (living beings, vehicles etc. in some direction)
parole.testo: From Middle High German drengen, from Old High German drengen, from Proto-West Germanic *þrangwijan, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat, press”). From Middle High German du, duo, dū, from Old High German dū (akin to Old Saxon thū and English thou), itself from Proto-West Germanic *þū, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

From Middle High German dult, tult, from Old High German tuld (“idle period”), from Proto-West Germanic *dulþi, from Proto-Germanic *dulþiz (“feast, Easter”), of unknown origin. Compare Gothic 𐌳𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (dulþs, “feast”).

From Middle High German tump, from Old High German tumb, from Proto-West Germanic *dumb, from Proto-Germanic *dumbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-. From Middle High German tunc, tunge, from Old High German tung, tunga, from Proto-West Germanic *dungu, from Proto-Germanic *dungō, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ- (“to cover”). The word also meant in High German—and it seems exclusively in Low German (compare Old Saxon dung)—a dwelling or storage

From Middle High German durst, from Old High German durst, thurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”). Akin to Old Dutch thursti (modern dorst), Old English þurst (modern thirst), and Old Saxon thurst.

parole.significato: to desiccate, to dry (especially for preservation of foodstuff)
parole.testo: From Middle High German derren, from Old High German derren, from Proto-Germanic *þarzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *torséyeti, thematic causative present of Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”). Cognate with Latin torreō. Compare also dorren from the same root but without the umlaut.
From Middle High German dunken, from Old High German dunken, from Proto-West Germanic *þunkijan, from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną.

From Middle High German dürre, from Old High German durrī, from Proto-West Germanic *þurʀī, from Proto-Germanic *þursuz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ters-. Equivalent to dürr (“dry”) + -e (“-ness”).

The adjective is from Middle High German eben, from Old High German eban, the adverb from ebano; from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz and its adverb equivalent. Cognate with Low German even, Dutch even, effen, English even, Danish jævn.

From Middle High German ëber, from Old High German ëbur, from Proto-West Germanic *ebur, from Proto-Germanic *eburaz, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-r-. Cognate with Dutch ever, Latin aper, Serbo-Croatian vepar. Despite the similarity in form and meaning, not related to obsolete dialectal B
From Middle High German ecke, from Old High German egga, from Proto-West Germanic *aggju, from Proto-Germanic *agjō. Compare English edge.
From Middle High German edel, adel, from Old High German adal, from Proto-West Germanic *aþal, Proto-Germanic *aþalaz, see also Old English æþel- (> English athel), Old Norse aðall.

From Middle High German egel(e), from Old High German egala (8th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *egulā, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *egulaz. Cognate to Dutch echel. Further related with Ancient Greek ἔχις (ékhis), Armenian իժ (iž).

parole.significato: marriage (state of being married; life as a married couple)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ē, ēwe, from Old High German ēwa, from Proto-West Germanic *aiw, from Proto-Germanic *aiwǭ, *aiwaz (“law, custom”).

From Middle High German ēre, from Old High German ēra (“honour, fame, sense of honour”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀu, from Proto-Germanic *aizō. Cognate with Old Norse eir (“pardon, gentleness”), Old Saxon ēra (“honour, protection, pardon, gift”), Old English ār (“honour, help, pardon”), and Lati

Inherited from Middle High German ei and Old High German ei, from Proto-West Germanic *aij, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm. Cognate with Yiddish איי (ey), Dutch ei, West Frisian aai, English ey and egg, Danish æg.

From Middle High German īwe, from Old High German īwa, from Proto-West Germanic *īwā, īhwā, *īhu, from Proto-Germanic *īwō, *īhwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw-. Cognate with dated Dutch ijf, English yew, Lithuanian ievà, Russian ива (iva). Middle High German postvocalic -w- was normally lost.
Inherited from Middle High German eichurne, eichorn. See Eichhörnchen for more.
From Middle High German eit, from Old High German eid, from Proto-West Germanic *aiþ, from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz. Compare Dutch eed, English oath, Danish ed.

parole.significato: own, peculiar or private to someone, idiosyncratic, proper or proprietary
parole.testo: From Middle High German eigen, from Old High German eigan, from Proto-West Germanic *aigan, from Proto-Germanic *aiganaz, the past participle of Proto-Germanic *aiganą. Cognate with Dutch eigen, English own.
From Middle High German īlaé, from Old High German īla, from Proto-West Germanic *īlu, from Proto-Germanic *īlō (“rush, haste”).
From Middle High German ein, from Old High German ein. Compare Low German en, een, ein, Dutch een, English one, Danish en, Norwegian Nynorsk ein.

parole.significato: indicating (concrete or abstract/metaphorical) motion into something
parole.testo: Related to in, from Old High German in, from Proto-Germanic *in, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. Compare ein- and English in-.

parole.significato: to commence, initiate, trigger, instigate, start
parole.testo: From Middle High German īnleiten, from Old High German inleiten, from Proto-West Germanic *inlaidijan, from Proto-Germanic *inlaidijaną. Equivalent to ein- + leiten. Cognates include Dutch inleiden and English inlead.

From Middle High German īs, from Old High German īs, from Proto-West Germanic *īs, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-. Etymology 1, noun sense 2 is a semantic loan from French glace.

From Middle High German īsen, īsern, from Old High German īsarn, from Proto-West Germanic *īsarn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną, from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Cognate with Dutch ijzer, Alemannic German Ise, English iron, Danish jern.

From Middle High German elch, elhe, from Old High German elaho, elho, elcho (hapax elach), from Proto-West Germanic *elh(ō), from Proto-Germanic *elhaz. Inherited from Middle High German ende, from Old High German enti, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.
From Middle High German enkel, from Old High German enkil, enchil, Proto-West Germanic *ankil, *ankul, from Proto-Germanic *ankulaz (“ankle”). Cognate with Dutch enkel, English ankle.

parole.significato: Inseparable verb prefix indicating removing something from the object, from, away from, off.

parole.significato: inheritance; heritage; legacy; bequest (property that is bequeathed and inherited)
parole.testo: From Middle High German erbe, from Old High German erbi, from Proto-West Germanic *arbī, from Proto-Germanic *arbiją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“to change ownership”). Cognate with Dutch erf (“yard”), obsolete English erf. Related to German Arbeit (“work”).
From Middle High German erbe, from Old High German erbo, arbeo, from Proto-Germanic *arbijô.

parole.significato: to inherit (as a bequest or by genetics)

By surface analysis, Erde (“earth”) + Beere (“berry”); from Middle High German ërtbere, from Old High German ërdberi, from Proto-Germanic *erþōbazją. Akin to Dutch aardbei, Danish jordbær. Compare Polish poziomka, Russian земляни́ка (zemljaníka) (related to земля́ (zemljá)).

From Middle High German ërde, from Old High German ërda, from Proto-West Germanic *erþu, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁érteh₂ (“earth”). Compare Dutch aarde, West Frisian ierde, Low German Eerde, English earth, Danish jord, Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸𐌰 (airþa).
From Middle High German ergëben, from Old High German irgëban, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgeban, Proto-Germanic *uzgebaną; cognate with obsolete English agive. Equivalent to er- + geben.

parole.significato: to raise, lift (one's arm, voice, glass, etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle High German erheben, from Old High German irheffen, irheven, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀhabbjan, from Proto-Germanic *uzhabjaną. Equivalent to er- + heben. Cognate with Middle Dutch erheffen (whence Dutch verheffen), Old Saxon āhebbian, Old English āhebban, Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌷𐌰𐍆𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ushafjan).

From Middle High German erlouben, from Old High German irlouben, arlouben, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlaubijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzlaubijaną. Cognate with Old English ālīefan, ālȳfan (“to allow”). More at leave (“permission”).

From Middle High German erle, from Old High German erila, from Proto-West Germanic *aliʀu, from Proto-Germanic *alizō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élis-. Compare Dutch els, English alder, Danish el, Norwegian older, Icelandic elri.
From Middle High German erlœsen, from Old High German irlōsen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlausijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzlausijaną. By surface analysis, er + lösen (“to loosen”).

parole.significato: to determine (something) through advice or empathy
parole.testo: From Middle High German erraten, from Old High German irrātan, arrātan, urrātan, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀrādan, from Proto-Germanic *uzrēdaną (“to guess”). Equivalent to er- + raten (“advise, recommend; guess”). Cognate with English arread.
From Middle High German ersuochen, from Old High German irsuohhen, ursuohhen, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀsōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzsōkijaną. Equivalent to er- + suchen.

From Middle High German vach, from Old High German fah, from Proto-West Germanic *fak, from Proto-Germanic *faką.

From Old High German vart, from Proto-West Germanic *fardi, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz, derived from *faraną (“to go, travel”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“going, passage”). Cognate with Dutch vaart, Swedish färd, English fard, ferd. Equivalent to a deverbal from fahren.
From Middle High German valke, from Old High German falco, from Proto-West Germanic *falkō, from Proto-Germanic *falkô.

From Middle High German varwe, from Old High German farawa, from Proto-West Germanic *faru, from Proto-Germanic *farwō.
From Middle High German farre, from Old High German farro, from Proto-West Germanic *farʀō, from Proto-Germanic *farzô.

parole.significato: to gird, to surround, to confine into a form
parole.testo: From Middle High German vaȥȥen, from Old High German faȥȥōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fatōn, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną (“to fetch, hold”). Cognate with English fetch.

From Middle High German vast, vaste, from Old High German fasto (“solidly, strictly, securely”), from Proto-West Germanic *fastō, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz. parole.significato: to sweep (to clean with a broom)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vëgen, from Old High German fëgōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fegōn.

From Middle High German vēch (“spotted, mottled fur”), from the adjective vēch, vēhe, vē (“multicoloured”, whence obsolete German fech, feh), from Old High German fēh, from Proto-West Germanic *faih, from Proto-Germanic *faihaz. Cognate with Scots faw.

parole.significato: venal, capable of being bribed or prostituted
parole.testo: From Middle High German veile, from Old High German feili (“for sale”), from Proto-West Germanic *failī. Possibly merged with a descendant of Proto-Germanic *falaz, but this is uncertain. Old High German fali is only attested once in a text that uses ai for ei, thus quite plausibly a mere scribal er
From Middle High German fīle, fīhel, from Old High German fīla, fī(h)ila, fīhala, from Proto-West Germanic *fį̄hlu, from Proto-Germanic *finhlō.

parole.significato: enemy, fiend, foe (male or of unspecified gender)

parole.significato: field (plot of open land, especially one used to grow crops)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vëlt, from Old High German fëld, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu, from Proto-Germanic *felþą, from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂-. Cognates include Dutch veld and English field.

From Middle High German vels, from Old High German felis, from Proto-West Germanic *falis, from Proto-Germanic *falisaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pels-, *pelis- (“rock, cliff”). From Middle High German vest, from Old High German festi, from Proto-West Germanic *fast, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz; see there for cognates and further etymology.

From Middle High German viur, from Old High German fiur, from Proto-West Germanic *fuir. Cognate with Dutch vuur, Low German Füer, West Frisian fjoer, English fire, Danish fyr.

From Middle High German vlëc, from Old High German flec, flek, from Proto-West Germanic *flekkō, from Proto-Germanic *flekka- (“spot, mark”). Cognate with Dutch vlek, English fleck.

parole.testo: From Middle High German flīȥ, vlīȥ, from Old High German flīȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *flītan (“to strive”), from Proto-Germanic *flītaz, *flītiz (“strife, zeal, effort, diligence”). Cognate with German Low German Fliet, Dutch vlijt, Saterland Frisian Fliet, English flite.

parole.significato: to fly; to travel by air
parole.testo: From Middle High German vliegen, Old High German fliogan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleugan, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *plewk-. Compare Bavarian fliagn, Dutch vliegen, Low German flegen, English fly, Danish flyve.
From Middle High German vliehen, from Old High German fliohan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleuhan, from Proto-Germanic *fleuhaną. Cognate with Dutch vlieden and English flee.
From Middle High German vliez, from Old High German flioz, from Proto-West Germanic *fleut, from Proto-Germanic *fleutą. Doublet of Fleet. Related with fließen, Fluss.
From Middle High German vlieȥen, from Old High German flioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleutan, from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną, akin to English fleet (verb), Old Saxon fliotan and Dutch vlieten.
From Middle High German vluochen, from Old High German fluohhon, from Proto-West Germanic *flōkan, from Proto-Germanic *flōkaną. Cognate with Dutch vloeken.

From Middle High German vluȥ, from Old High German fluȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *fluti, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, ultimately from the same root of fließen (“to flow”). Not cognate with Latin fluvius, which derives instead from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlewH-.

parole.significato: flow, flood, high tide (rising movement of the tide; the time around when it reaches its peak)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vluot, Old High German fluot, from Proto-West Germanic *flōdu, from Proto-Germanic *flōduz. Compare Dutch vloed, English flood, Danish flod, Icelandic flóð.

From older flez, from Middle High German vletz, vletze (“threshing floor”), from Old High German flezzi, from Proto-West Germanic *flati, from Proto-Germanic *flatją (“floor”). Cognate with Low German Flett, Old English flett, Old Norse flet.

From Middle High German vrostec, from Old High German frostag, from Proto-West Germanic *frostag, from Proto-Germanic *frustagaz, equivalent to Frost + -ig.

From Middle High German vuhs, from Old High German fuhs, from Proto-West Germanic *fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *púḱsos (“the tailed one”), from *puḱ- (“tail”). Cognate with English fox, Sanskrit पुच्छ (púccha).
From Middle High German funke, vunke (also ablauted as vanke), from Old High German funko, funcho, from Proto-West Germanic *funkō, from Proto-Germanic *funkô. More at English spunk.

From Middle High German vuozspor, from Old High German fuozspor, from Proto-West Germanic *fōtspor, from Proto-Germanic *fōtspurą, equivalent to Fuß + Spur.

From Middle High German gesamt, gesament, from Old High German gisamanōt, from samanōn (“to gather, collect”), from Proto-West Germanic *samnōn, from Proto-Germanic *samnōną (“to bring together”).

From Middle High German geschirre (“harness, gear”), from Old High German giskirri, giscirri (literally “the trimmed (thing)”), from skeran (“to shear”), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną. Cognate with Alemannic German Geschirr.
From Middle High German stuppe, stüppe, from Old High German stuppi, from Proto-West Germanic *stubbju, from Proto-Germanic *stubjuz (“dust”).

From Middle High German gesunt, from Old High German gisunt, from Proto-West Germanic *gasund, a prefixed form of *sund, from Proto-Germanic *sundaz. Cognates include Bavarian gsund, Alemannic German gsund, Dutch gezond, English sound.
From Middle High German *getrüebet, from Old High German gitruobit, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbid, from Proto-Germanic *drōbidaz.

From Middle High German gewis, from Old High German giwis, from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz (“known, certain, sure”). Cognate with Dutch wis, English iwis.

From Middle High German gloube, geloube, from Old High German giloubo, from Proto-West Germanic *galaubō, from Proto-Germanic *galaubô. More at glauben (“to believe”).

Inherited from Middle High German gelīch, from Old High German gilīh, from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.

From Middle High German klucken, from Old High German klokkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klukkwōn, from Proto-Germanic *klukkwōną, of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate with Dutch klokken, English cluck. The g- by dissimilation.
From Middle High German glüejen, from Old High German gluoen. Compare Dutch gloeien, English glow, Danish glo.

From Middle High German golt, from Old High German gold, from Proto-West Germanic *golþ, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą.

From Middle High German got, from Old High German got, from Proto-West Germanic *god, from Proto-Germanic *gudą. Compare Dutch god, English god, Danish gud, Gothic 𐌲𐌿𐌸 (guþ).

From Middle High German grap, from Old High German grap, from Proto-West Germanic *grab, from Proto-Germanic *grabą, *grabō (“grave, trench, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrābʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”). From Middle High German grasen, from Old High German grasōn, from Proto-West Germanic *grasōn. Equivalent to Gras (“grass”) + -en (verbal suffix). Cognate with English graze.

parole.significato: to grab; to grasp; to grip (something)

parole.significato: aged, very old, especially when decrepit or senile

From Middle High German griez, from Old High German grioz, from Proto-Germanic *greutą. Akin to Old Norse grjót, English grit.

parole.significato: grasp, reach (act of trying to grab)

From Middle High German gotinne, from Old High German gutin, from Proto-West Germanic *gudinī, from Proto-Germanic *gudinī. Cognate with Dutch godin, Old English gyden, Swedish gudinna. By surface analysis, Gott + -in.

From Middle High German has(e), from Old High German haso, from Proto-West Germanic *hasō, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from an Indo-European root originally meaning grey.

parole.significato: skin, hide of a person, animal or (part of a) plant
parole.testo: From Middle High German hūt, from Old High German hūt, from Proto-West Germanic *hūdi, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH-.

From Middle High German heften, from Old High German heften, from Proto-West Germanic *haftijan, from Proto-Germanic *haftijaną.

parole.significato: home, one’s dwelling, the place where one is at home
parole.testo: From Middle High German heim, from Old High German heim, from Proto-West Germanic *haim. Cognate with Dutch heem, English home, Danish hjem.

From Middle High German heizen, from Old High German heizen, from Proto-West Germanic *haitijan, from Proto-Germanic *haitijaną.

parole.significato: to help (someone); to assist; to aid
parole.testo: From Middle High German hëlfen, from Old High German hëlfan, from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp-. Cognate with Low German helpen, Dutch helpen, English help, Danish hjælpe, Norwegian Bokmål hjelpe.

parole.significato: back; indicates a reversing or inverse of an action
parole.testo: From Middle High German rücke, from Old High German rucki, from Proto-West Germanic *hrugi, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz.

parole.significato: to wrinkle (especially a part of the face, the nose in particular, to show disapproval)
parole.testo: From Middle High German rümpfen, from Old High German (h)rimpfan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrimpan, from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to wrinkle”).

parole.significato: hall or large room (chiefly for gatherings or performances by large groups of people)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sal, from Old High German sal, sali, seli, from Proto-West Germanic *sali, from Proto-Germanic *saliz, *salą, from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“human settlement, village, dwelling”). Cognate with Dutch zaal, Swedish sal, Old English sele, Russian село́ (seló). Also cognate wit

From Middle High German sāt, from Old High German sāt, from Proto-West Germanic *sādi, from Proto-Germanic *sēdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *sētis-, *seh₁tis, from *seh₁- (“to sow”). Compare English seed, Low German Saad, Hunsrik Soot, Dutch zaad, Danish sæd.

From Middle High German sache, from Old High German sahha, from Proto-West Germanic *saku, from Proto-Germanic *sakō. Cognate with Bavarian Såch, Yiddish זאַך (zakh), German Low German Sake, Low German Sake, Dutch zaak, Afrikaans saak, English sake, Danish sag, Swedish sak.

parole.significato: Saxon (native or inhabitant of Saxony, Germany) (usually male)
parole.testo: From Middle High German Sahse, from Old High German Sahso, from Proto-West Germanic *Sahsō (“Saxon”).

parole.significato: sack (large bag, especially one made of fabric)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sac, from Old High German sac, from Proto-West Germanic *sakku, from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz, from Latin saccus. Cognate with Dutch zak, English sack. From Middle High German sage, from Old High German saga, from Proto-West Germanic *sagā, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ.

From Middle High German sagen, from Old High German sagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ-. Cognate with Bavarian sogn, Alemannic German säge, Low German seggen, Dutch zeggen, English say, Danish sige, Swedish säga.

From Middle High German seite, from Old High German seita (also seito m), from Proto-West Germanic *saidā, *saidō, from Proto-Germanic *saidô (“string, cord”). In the 17th century, the ⟨ei⟩ was changed to the homophonous ⟨ai⟩, in order to distinguish this word from Seite. Derived from Seite original
From Middle High German salbe, from Old High German salba, from Proto-West Germanic *salbu, from Proto-Germanic *salbō.
From Middle High German salben, from Old High German salbon, from Proto-West Germanic *salbōn, from Proto-Germanic *salbōną. Equivalent to Salbe + -en.

Inherited from Middle High German salz, from Old High German salz (akin to Old Saxon salt, Old Dutch salt, Old English sealt, Old Norse salt), from Proto-West Germanic *salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Compare Dutch zout, English salt, Danish salt. The Inte
From Middle High German sām, sāme, from Old High German sāmo, from Proto-West Germanic *sāmō, from Proto-Germanic *sēmô, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.

From Middle High German sant, from Old High German sant, from Proto-West Germanic *sand, *samd, from Proto-Germanic *sandaz, *samdaz. The forms with -n- are due to early assimilation. The more original form with -m- is attested in Middle High German sambt, sampt, which survives in some Bavarian dial
From Middle High German sat, from Old High German sat, from Proto-West Germanic *sad, from Proto-Germanic *sadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂-. Compare Dutch zat, English sad, Danish sat.

From Middle High German satel, from Old High German satal, from Proto-West Germanic *sadul, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz. Cognate with Old Norse sǫðull, Old English sadol, Dutch zadel, English saddle.
From Middle High German sateln, satelen, satlen, from Old High German satulōn, from Proto-West Germanic *sadulōn, from Proto-Germanic *sadulōną. By surface analysis, Sattel (“saddle”) + -n.
From Middle High German sū, from Old High German sū, from Proto-West Germanic *sū.

From Middle High German sūr, from Old High German sūr, from Proto-West Germanic *sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūraz, from Proto-Indo-European *súHros. Cognate to Low German suur, Dutch zuur, English sour, Danish sur, Swedish sur.

parole.significato: to scrape, shave, plane, pare (remove or reduce the outer layer of something with a sharp object)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schaben, from Old High German skaban, from Proto-West Germanic *skaban, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scrape, scratch”). Cognate with Dutch schaven, English shave, Danish skave, Swedish skava, Icelandic skafa, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (skaban).

From Middle High German schade, from Old High German skado, from Proto-West Germanic *skaþō, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô. Compare Dutch schade, Low German Schaden, Schaad, English scathe, Danish skade, Swedish skada.
From Middle High German schaf, from Old High German scaf, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą. Doublet of Schapp. Cognate with Dutch schap and Swedish skåp.

From Middle High German schale, from Old High German scala, from Proto-West Germanic *skalu, from Proto-Germanic *skalō. Cognate with Dutch schaal (“shell”) and English shale. Also related with Dutch schil, English shell.

From Middle High German schal, from Old High German scal, from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Dutch schal and Swedish skall. Compare English low (“to moo”).

From Middle High German schallen, from the root of Schall (“sound”). The Grimms have it as corrupt form of Middle High German schëllen (inflected schal, geschollen), from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”).

parole.significato: shame (uncomfortable feeling at one's own impropriety or at the exposure of something private; but not in the sense of…
parole.testo: From Middle High German schame, from Old High German scama, from Proto-West Germanic *skamu, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European [Term?]. Compare Dutch schaamte, English shame, Danish skam.

parole.significato: disgrace, infamy, dishonour (state or result considered highly disreputable for whoever is responsible)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schande, from Old High German scanta, from Proto-West Germanic *skandu, from Proto-Germanic *skandō (“shame, disgrace”). Cognate with Yiddish שאַנדע (shande), English shand, Dutch schande.
From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German scara (“troop”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō. Cognate with English share, Swedish skara.

parole.significato: sharp; able to cut (of a knife, edge)
parole.testo: From Middle High German scharpf, from Old High German scarf, from Proto-West Germanic *skarp, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Compare Low German scharp, Dutch scherp, English sharp, Danish skarp.
From Middle High German schoup, from Old High German scoub, from Proto-West Germanic *skaub, from Proto-Germanic *skauba-. Ultimately related to schieben (“to shove”). Doublet of Schof.

parole.significato: to watch, to view (a movie or other performance)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schouwen, from Old High German scouwōn, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, see, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to heed, look, feel, take note of”). Cognate with Old English scēawian (“to look at, examine, show”). Compare English show.
From Middle High German schūr, from Old High German scūr, from Proto-West Germanic *skūr, from Proto-Germanic *skūrō. Cognate with Dutch schoer, English shower, Swedish skur.
From Middle High German schūm, from Old High German scūm, from Proto-West Germanic *skūm, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz. Cognate to English scum.

From Middle High German schībe, from Old High German skība, from Proto-West Germanic *skībā, from Proto-Germanic *skībǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, part, divide, separate”). Cognate with Dutch schijf, English shive, sheave, skive, Old Norse skífa.

From Middle High German schīze, from Old High German *skizi, from Proto-West Germanic *skiti, from Proto-Germanic *skītaz, *skitiz, from Proto-Indo-European *skeyd- (“to part”). Germanic cognates include English shit, Low German Schiet, Dutch schijt, West Frisian skyt, Swedish skit. Standard High Ge

From Middle High German schīȥen, from Old High German *skīȥan (attested in biskīȥan), from Proto-West Germanic *skītan, from Proto-Germanic *skītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skeyd-, *sḱeyd- (“to part with, separate, cut off”). parole.significato: to give as a present, to gift
parole.testo: From Middle High German schenken, from Old High German scenken, from Proto-West Germanic *skankijan (“to pour, serve”).

parole.significato: to cut back something that grows
parole.testo: From Middle High German schërn, from Old High German skëran, from Proto-West Germanic *skeran, from Proto-Germanic *skeraną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Akin to Low German scheren, Dutch scheren, West Frisian skarre, English shear, Danish skære.
From Middle High German scherge, from Old High German skerio (“troop leader”), from Old High German scara (“troop”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō.

From Middle High German schiech (“despondent, frightening, ugly”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh (“shy, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, fearful”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian skjou (“shy”), Dutch schuw (“shy”), English shy, Danish sky (“shy”), and doublet of schiech.

parole.significato: to shy, to balk at (to physically refuse going near a source of fear, especially of animals)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schiuhen, from Old High German sciuhen, from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhan, from the Proto-Germanic adjective *skiuhaz (“shy”). By surface analysis, scheu + -en. Doublet of scheuchen. Compare Dutch schuwen.

From Middle High German schiure, from Old High German skiura, from Proto-West Germanic *skūru, from Proto-Germanic *skūrō. Originally the predominant High German word, except in the north-east. Cognate with Dutch schuur.

From Middle High German schieben, from Old High German skioban, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuban, from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ-. Cognate with Low German schuven, Dutch schuiven, English shove, Danish skubbe.

From Middle High German schilhen, from Old High German scilihen, from Proto-West Germanic *skilhijan, from Proto-Germanic *skilhijaną, *skilhwijaną (“to squint”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to bend; crook”). Related to Dutch scheel (“squinty; squint-eyed”), Old English sċeolh (“slanted; obl

From Middle High German schinbein, schinebein, from Old High German skinabein, from Proto-West Germanic *skinubain, from Proto-Germanic *skinōbainą. Equivalent to Schiene + Bein. Compare Hunsrik Schienbeen, Dutch scheenbeen, English shinbone, Danish skinneben, Swedish skenben.

From Middle High German schif, from Old High German skif (“ship, barrel, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“ship, hollow object”). Cognate with Dutch schild, English shield, Danish skjold. The -ld-

From Middle High German schinke, from Old High German scinco, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō, from Proto-Germanic *skinkô, *skinkō (“shank; thigh”). From Middle High German slac, from Old High German slag, from Proto-West Germanic *slagi (“a blow, strike”). Perhaps cognate to English slug (“hard blow”).

parole.testo: The more original form is schlah(e)n, from Middle High German slahen, from Old High German slahan, from Proto-West Germanic *slahan, from Proto-Germanic *slahaną. From Middle High German slecken, from Old High German *slikkon, from Proto-West Germanic *slikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *slikkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”). Cognate with Bavarian schleckn and Dutch slikken.

From Middle High German slēhe, from Old High German slēha, from Proto-West Germanic *slaihā, from Proto-Germanic *slaihǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *sléh₃ikos (“bluish”). Cognate with Dutch slee, English sloe, Swedish slån, and probably with Proto-Slavic *sliva (“plum”), whence Russian сли́ва (slíva)

parole.significato: to move in a quiet and inconspicuous manner, hence often slowly and/or ducked: to crawl, to sneak, to steal, to prowl,…
parole.testo: From Middle High German slīchen, from Old High German slīhhan. Compare also English slink, though formally unrelated. Cognate with English slick.

parole.significato: to whet, grind (smooth and/or sharpen a surface by abrasion)
parole.testo: From Middle High German slīfen (strong verb), from Old High German slīfan, from Proto-West Germanic *slīpan, from Proto-Germanic *slīpaną (“to slide, to whet”). parole.significato: to settle, to mediate (a dispute or argument)
parole.testo: From Middle High German slihten, from Old High German slihten, from Proto-West Germanic *slihtijan, from Proto-Germanic *slihtijaną. By surface analysis, schlicht + -en.

parole.significato: to shut; to close; to shut down
parole.testo: From Middle High German slieȥen, from Old High German slioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *sleutan, from Proto-Germanic *slūtaną, *sleutaną (“to lock, shut”). Cognate with Old Saxon slūtan, Dutch sluiten, English slot.

parole.significato: bad, terrible, serious (seriously bad), dire, horrible, awful
parole.testo: From earlier slim, from Middle High German slimp (“slanting, awry”), from Old High German slimb, from Proto-West Germanic *slimb, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz (“oblique, crooked”). Compare English slim (“thin”), Dutch slim (“clever, smart”), Middle Dutch slim (“bad, crooked”).

parole.significato: loop, noose (rope or similar material fashioned into or forming a loop, typically small to mid-sized)
parole.testo: From Middle High German slinge, from Old High German slinga, from Proto-West Germanic *slingwan, from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist”). Compare schlingen and English sling.
From Middle High German slingen, from Old High German slingan, from Proto-West Germanic *slingwan, from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to twist”). Compare English sling.
From Middle High German slitzen, from Old High German slizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *slittjan, from Proto-Germanic *slittjaną.

parole.significato: to throw; to fling; to hurl
parole.testo: From Middle High German smīzen, from Old High German smīzan, from Proto-West Germanic *smītan, from Proto-Germanic *smītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *smeyd-. Cognate with Dutch smijten, Low German smieten, English smite, Danish smide, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐌼𐌴𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (bismeitan).

From Middle High German smëlzen, from Old High German smëlzan, from Proto-West Germanic *smeltan, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną. Akin to Old Saxon smeltan. Cognate with English smelt, Danish smelte, Dutch smelten, German Low German smölten. Through the meaning of soften: compare Old Church Slavonic
From Middle High German smẹlzen, from Old High German smẹlzen, from Proto-West Germanic *smaltijan, from Proto-Germanic *smaltijaną; causative of the previous verb.

parole.significato: fat or lard, usually of a pig
parole.testo: From Middle High German smer, from Old High German smero, from Proto-West Germanic *smeru, from Proto-Germanic *smerwą, from Proto-Indo-European *smérus.

parole.significato: physical pain, ache (practically, as a sensation)
parole.testo: From Middle High German smerze m or f, from Old High German smerza f, smerzo m, from Proto-West Germanic *smertan. Cognate with English smart, Dutch smart.

parole.significato: to hurt, to ache (to cause physical/bodily pain, often of parts of one's own body)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schmërzen, from Old High German smërzan, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with Dutch smarten, English smart, Low German smerten, Danish smerte, Swedish smärta.
From Middle High German smit, from Old High German smid, from Proto-West Germanic *smiþ, from Proto-Germanic *smiþaz.

From Late Middle High German smide (15th c.), alteration of older smitte, from Old High German smitta (early also smiththa, seldom smidda), from Proto-West Germanic *smiþþjā, from Proto-Germanic *smiþjǭ. Cognate with Dutch smidse, English smithy. The modern form, which had displaced Schmitte by the
From Middle High German smiegen, from Old High German smiogan (“to pull up, contract, snuggle”), from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan, from Proto-Germanic *smeuganą.

parole.significato: to smear, to spread (a cream or similar substance across across a surface)
parole.testo: From Middle High German smirn, from older smirwen, from Old High German smirwen, from Proto-West Germanic *smirwijan, from Proto-Germanic *smirwijaną, derived from *smerwą, whence dated German Schmer (“fat”). The loss of -w- is mostly a Central German development; compare fahl and falb, etc. Cognate
From Middle High German snê, from Old High German snēo, from Proto-West Germanic *snaiw.
From Middle High German snīen, from Old High German snīwan, from Proto-West Germanic *snīwan, from Proto-Germanic *snīwaną.

From Middle High German snël, from Old High German snël (“nimble, brave, quick, lively”), from Proto-West Germanic *snel, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, bold, quick”). Cognate with Dutch snel, Low German snell, English snell. More at snell.

From Middle High German schopf, akin to Old High German scuft, from Proto-West Germanic *skuft, from Proto-Germanic *skuftą. Akin to Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐍆𐍄 (skuft, “hair of the head”), compare English sheaf, scruff, Old Norse skopt (“hair of the head”), skauf (“fox's tail”), North Frisian skuft (“back of the
From Middle High German schoȥ n, from Old High German scoȥ n, from Proto-West Germanic *skot, from Proto-Germanic *skutą.

parole.significato: cabinet (storage closet either separate from, or built into, a wall), or (specifically):
parole.testo: From Late Middle High German schranc, from Old High German scranc, from Proto-West Germanic *skrank, from Proto-Germanic *skrankaz (“grid, barrier”), probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). Cognate with German Low German Schrank (“barrier, barricade”).

parole.significato: to grind, chip, crush something coarsely
parole.testo: From Middle High German schrōten, from Old High German skrōtan, from Proto-West Germanic *skraudan, from Proto-Germanic *skraudaną.
From Middle High German schult, from Old High German sculd, from Proto-West Germanic *skuldi, from Proto-Germanic *skuldiz. Cognate with obsolete English shild (“debt, fault, guilt”).
From Middle High German schurz (“apron”), substantivization of schurz (“short”), from Old High German scurz, from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz. Compare Schürze.

From Middle High German schuȥ, from Old High German scuȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *skuti; whence English shoot and skeet. Cognate with Dutch scheut, Old English scyte, Icelandic skutur. Related to schießen and Schoss.

From Middle High German swāger, from Old High German swāger, swāgur, from Proto-West Germanic *swāgr, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz (“husband's brother”), from Proto-Indo-European *swēḱurós (“brother-in-law”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“husband's father”).
From Middle High German swamme, swam, swamp, from Old High German swamp, from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz. See also Old English swamm.

From Middle High German swan, from Old High German swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”), from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). Compare Low German Swaan, Dutch zwaan, English swan, Swedish svan.

From the adjective schwarz, from Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”). Compare German schwarz, Dutch zwart, English swart.

parole.significato: black, reflecting little or no light
parole.testo: From Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”). Compare Dutch zwart, English swart and swarthy, West Frisian swart, Danish sort, Yiddish שוואַרץ (shvarts).

parole.significato: A mediaeval woodwind instrument, similar to a recorder, with three finger holes.
parole.testo: From Middle High German swegel, swegele, from Old High German swegala, from Proto-West Germanic *sweglā, *sweglu, from Proto-Germanic *sweglō.
From Middle High German sweifen, from Old High German sweifan, from Proto-West Germanic *swaipan, from Proto-Germanic *swaipaną.

parole.significato: to wave, to brandish (a long item, e.g. a flag or sword)
parole.testo: From Middle High German swenken, Old High German swenken, from Proto-West Germanic *swankijan, from Proto-Germanic *swankijaną (“cause to swing”).
From Middle High German swær, from Old High German swār, from Proto-West Germanic *swār, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy, grave, serious”).
Middle High German swære, from Old High German swārī, from Proto-West Germanic *swārī, from Proto-Germanic *swērį̄; equivalent to schwer + -e. Cognate with British English sweer.
From Middle High German swæren, from Old High German swārēn, from Proto-West Germanic *swārēn, from Proto-Germanic *swērāną.

From Middle High German swëster, from Old High German swëster, from Proto-Germanic *swestēr. Compare Low German swester, Dutch zuster, English sister, Danish søster, Swedish syster.

From Middle High German swil, from Old High German swil, from Proto-West Germanic *swili, from Proto-Germanic *swiliz, related to German schwellen.

parole.significato: to swim (to use swimming motions to move in the water)
parole.testo: From Middle High German swimmen, from Old High German swimman, from Proto-West Germanic *swimman, from Proto-Germanic *swimmaną. Compare Low German swimmen, Dutch zwemmen, English swim, Danish svømme.
From Proto-West Germanic *swippjan (“to move quickly; to sweep; to whip”), from Proto-Germanic *swipōną (“to move”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyb- (“to bend, sway, sweep, swerve, swing, turn”).

parole.significato: to sweat; to perspire (of living beings)

parole.significato: to muddle, bedim, blear, blur (make something turbid or unclear)
parole.testo: From Middle High German trüeben, from Old High German truoben, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbijan, from Proto-Germanic *drōbijaną.

parole.significato: to do (to perform or execute an action)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tuon, from Old High German tuon, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, set, place”). Cognate with English do.

parole.significato: to avoid, bypass, to go around (a physical obstacle)

From Middle High German verboten, from Old High German firbotan, from Proto-West Germanic *furibodan, from Proto-Germanic *furibudanaz.

From Middle High German verkomen, from Old High German *firkweman, from Proto-West Germanic *frakweman, from Proto-Germanic *frakwemaną. Equivalent to ver- + kommen.

parole.significato: to leave, to abandon; to depart, to forsake
parole.testo: From Middle High German verlāzen, Old High German firlāzan, from Proto-West Germanic *fralātan, from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną. Cognate with Dutch verlaten, archaic and/or dialectal English forlet, and Middle Low German vorlaten. Equivalent to ver- (“for-”) + lassen (“let, leave”).

From Middle High German vernemen, from Old High German firneman, from Proto-West Germanic *franeman, from Proto-Germanic *franemaną (“to take away”), equivalent to ver- + nehmen.

From Middle High German wanne, Old High German wanne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannā, *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan. Cognate with English when.

From Middle High German weide, from Old High German weida, from Proto-West Germanic *waiþu, from Proto-Germanic *waiþō. Cognate to Dutch weide (“pasture”).

parole.significato: to dedicate to a cause or purpose
parole.testo: From Middle High German wīhen, from Old High German wīhen, from Proto-West Germanic *wīhijan (“to hallow”), from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną (“to hallow”). Cognate with Dutch wijden.

From Middle High German wër, from Old High German wër, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaʀ. Related to wo.

From Middle High German wetzen, from Old High German wezzen, hwezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *hwattjan, from Proto-Germanic *hwatjaną (“to incite, sharpen”). Cognate with English whet.
